title: The bhog
hookLine: the close of a complete reading, with the last pages, Anand and Ardas

lines: HOW IT CLOSES HAS A SHAPE.
cards: The room has been quiet for days, one reader's voice after another. Now it's filling up. Cousins arrive from across town.

Somebody's grandmother is helped to a spot near the front. Children are hushed and sat down. The reader is close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and everyone has come to hear the last pages together.
A whole reading, whether it was unbroken or slow, is about to close. How it closes has a name, and a shape, and the shape carries its own teaching.

teach.h: BHOG: THE CLOSE OF A READING.
teach.b: The word is bhog. In Sikh use, it names the close of a complete reading of the Granth. First come the last pages.
Near the very end is a short passage called the Mundavani, the seal, by Guru Arjan.
In paraphrase: in this platter three things have been placed, truth, contentment and contemplation, and with them the Name, the support of all; whoever eats of it, whoever enjoys it, is saved.
So the Granth ends by describing itself as a meal. Everything read over those days turns out to have been a plate set before the sangat.
Communities differ on where the reading stops, at the Mundavani or carrying on through the Ragmala that follows it, and the code notes that difference and leaves it to custom.

teach.h: ANAND SAHIB, THE SONG OF BLISS.
teach.b: Then Anand Sahib is sung, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss. Anand means bliss, and the reading closes not with a sigh of relief but with joy.

teach.h: THE ARDAS, THEN A SHARED OFFERING.
teach.b: Then everyone stands for the Ardas, the prayer that remembers the Gurus and asks for the Guru's grace, and the reading is offered up.

A hukam is taken, and karah prashad, the sweet offering, is shared, which is tomorrow's story. Look at what the bhog refuses to do. It doesn't let the last page just run out, the way a phone call can drop.
It gathers people. It names what was received.
It gives thanks out loud. It asks forgiveness for any mistake in the reading. Then it feeds everyone.
A long reading ends not by stopping but by being completed.

how: At a bhog, family and sangat gather for the final pages of the Guru Granth Sahib; Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said standing, a hukam is taken and karah prashad is shared, often followed by a meal in the langar.

games.q: the last pages have been read and the room is full. what comes next at a bhog?
o: everyone leaves quietly; the reading is done.
Anand Sahib is sung and the Ardas said.
the reading starts over from the first page.
games.why: Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, then the Ardas, a hukam and karah prashad. the reading isn't stopped; it's completed.

practice: Bring to mind something that ended well, a goodbye at an airport, a last day at a job, a hard conversation that closed with a hug, and notice what made it good: who was there, what was said out loud.
Then think of something in your own life that's ending soon, and what it would take to end it well.
